34. From a decision of a Full Bench of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Ram Singha and others Vs. Shankar Dayal and another I.L.R. 50 Allahabad 965 (FB.) it appears that the rule of construction as laid down in the Colonial Sugar Refining Company Vs. Irving Case has been followed. This judgment provides us very valuable guidance on the consideration of the questions under reference. The question referred to the Full Bench was whether filing of an appeal is governed by the law obtaining at the date of the institution of a suit or by the law that may prevail at the date of the decision of it, or at the date of the filing of the appeal. The facts of the case in short are like this. The plaintiff Shankar Dayal brought a suit against Ram Singha and others for recovery of arrears of rent. The suit was instituted on July 12, 1926, when the Agra Tenancy Act of 1901 was still in force. The suit was decreed on December 23, 1926. An appeal was filed by the defendants before the Dist Judge, and the latter by his order dated August 31, 1927 returned the memorandum of appeal for presentation in the proper court. The memorandum of appeal was thereupon taken before the Collector of Etawah and the Collector being of the opinion that he had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal referred the case to the High Court under section 267 of the Agra Tenancy Act. The Bench before which the reference came for hearing referred it to Full Bench. The question for consideration was whether on coming into force of the new Tenancy Act, under which no appeal is provided, a defendant was deprived of his right of appeal provided in the old Tenancy Act. Sulaiman, A. C. J delivered the judgment of the Court. The learned Acting Chief Justice following the case of Colonial Sugar Refining Company Vs. living enunciated the principle of construction of a provision of a statute as under :- 

 46. The principles of law enunciated in Colonial Sugar Refining Co. Ltd. Vs. Irving Case have been applied by the Superior Courts in this Sub-Continent to cases where subsequent legislation did not take away the entire right of appeal but imposed certain onerous conditions on the lodgment of appeals. The case of Nagendra Nath Bose Vs. Mon Mohan Singh AIR 1931 Calcutta 100 is one of such cases. This decision of the Calcutta High Court was approved by the Supreme Court of India in Hossein Kasem Dada (India) Ltd. Vs Estate of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1953 Supreme Court 221. In the Calcutta case the restriction imposed on the admission of appeals in the proviso to section 174 (5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, was considered. Mitter, J. held as follows:- 

 47. In this context another case under the Bengal Tenancy Act considered by a Full Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Jatindra Nath De Vs. Jato Mahato and others, 50 C.W N. 502, may be referred to. Amendment of section 26F of the B.T. Act by B.T. (Amending) Act, 1938, gave rise to the question which was referred to the Full Bench. The question arose under the following circumstances. One Annapurna Debi had occupancy right in certain lands which were held by her as a tenant under the petitioner and his co-sharers. On May 20, 1938 she sold the holding by two separate registered kabalas to two different venders. Notice of those sales were served upon the landlords, including the petitioner on August 12, 1938. On October 26.1938 the petitioner as the co-sharer landlord filed two applications for pre-emption of both the transfers claiming to exercise his right of repurchase under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act as it stood before August 18,1938. The Munsif dismissed both these applications on the ground that there being no saving clause in the new section, that is, the rights that accrued under the old section 26F did not exist under the new section 26F came into force. Against this decision the landlord filed two revisional applications in the High Court. A Division Bench after hearing the Rules referred the following question to the Full Bench. 

 “Whether in case of transfer which occurred before the commencement of the Amended Bengal Tenancy Act of 1938, an immediate landlord who acquired a right to apply for pre-emption under section 26F of the old Act, could make an application under that section after the new Act came into force.” 

 55. On a careful examination of the facts of the case, it appears that the above noted observation is rather unwarranted, which is also in the nature of obiter dictum. The learned Chief Justice while following the decision of the Privy Council in the Colonial Sugar Refining Company Ltd. Vs. Irving case made the above observation. Nowhere in the judgment the learned Chief Justice raised any doubt about the soundness of the principles of law enunciated therein. The appeal before the Court arose out of an amendment of the East Bengal Civil Courts Act, 1887 changing forum of appeal in cases having valuation not exceeding Rs. 10,000/- from the High Court to District Judge. The learned Chief Justice after examining the different provisions of the amending. Act found that the amending Act was in essence retrospective. The learned Chief Justice concluded Stating:
